                                        PROJECT NO. 58000

      EVALUATION OF                                     §             BEFORE THE
       TRANSMISSION                                     §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
      COST RECOVERY                                     §              OF TEXAS


COMMENTS OF GRID RESILIENCE IN TEXAS ON JULY 10 PFP RE: EVALUATION
                OF TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY

        Grid Resilience in Texas (“GRIT”) appreciates the Commission’s careful consideration of
methodologies used to charge wholesale transmission costs to distribution providers under Public
Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §35.004(d).
        GRIT is comprised of a group of leading flexible generation and microgrid companies,
including Base Power Company, Bloom Energy, Critical Loop, Cummins Inc., ERock (formerly
Enchanted Rock), Generac Power Systems, Generate Capital, GridBeyond, Mainspring Energy, NW
Groupe, and PowerSecure Inc. These companies represent projects that encompass a spectrum of sizes,
from small-scale behind-the-meter (“BTM”) assets to large generation facilities utilizing various
technologies and fuel types. GRIT is improving energy reliability, resiliency, and affordability for
Texans by leveraging innovative solutions and stacking value streams for services to the grid and to
customers.


GENERAL COMMENTS
Load Flexibility
        Governor Abbott has directed the Commission and ERCOT to protect residential and
small-business customers from the infrastructure costs associated with data center expansion.1 The
Governor specifically called for data centers to fund the infrastructure required to serve them,
reduce costs for existing ratepayers, and add to Texas’ electric capacity rather than merely adding
demand. Although the Governor’s directive focuses on data centers, its underlying principles are
relevant to the broader large load framework under consideration. Existing customers should not
bear the costs of system upgrades constructed primarily to serve a new large load. At the same
time, the Commission should recognize that the most affordable transmission project is one that


1
 https://gov.texas.gov/uploads/files/press/Thomas_Gleeson_Pablo_Vegas_Data_Centers_Directive_Letter_to_PUC_
ERCOT_FINAL.pdf and https://www.utilitydive.com/news/texas-hits-pause-data-center-interconnections/827046/

                                               Page 1 of 8
 can be avoided or deferred. A flexible customer may require less firm transmission capacity than
an otherwise identical inflexible customer. A customer that installs dispatchable onsite generation,
commits to a defined maximum grid withdrawal level, or agrees to reduce load during peak system
conditions can reduce the amount of transmission service the grid must reliably provide. If those
commitments are incorporated into planning studies, they can improve utilization of existing
infrastructure and reduce the need for or timing of future transmission expansion.
          ERCOT has already developed mechanisms that distinguish energized load from firm grid
withdrawal and support Governor Abbott’s goals. Under the Batch Zero framework, a Provisional
Controllable Load Resource may be evaluated at defined low and maximum consumption levels,
while a Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network may combine a large load with onsite generation
subject to an enforceable withdrawal limit at the point of interconnection. ERCOT has explained
that these arrangements can accommodate load growth while reducing incremental transmission
dependency by netting onsite generation against load.2 These concepts provide a workable
foundation for a flexible transmission service option under which the customer’s withdrawal limit
or ability to curtail is used in applicable planning models.
          As a starting principle, the Commission’s rate design should accommodate and encourage
demand flexibility. The Commission’s proposed minimum billing demand would be based on the
greatest of contracted peak demand, maximum annual non-coincident peak (NCP) demand, or
actual 12 coincident peak (12CP) demand.3 As a standard practice, large loads will contract for as
much or greater demand than they require as firm. As a result, under the Commission’s proposal,
the minimum billing demand would likely be based on contracted peak demand. The Commission
should adopt targeted changes to its proposal and avoid charging a customer with dependable
onsite capacity as though the transmission system must serve its entire load under all conditions.
          Therefore, for a qualified flexible customer, the minimum billing demand should be based
on net firm withdrawal, i.e., the amount of demand that ERCOT and the applicable TSP must plan
to serve after accounting for enforceable limits, curtailment, and approved onsite generation. This
approach would better align with cost causation principles, preserve incentives for private
investment in dispatchable capacity, and protect existing ratepayers by reducing both cost shifting
and unnecessary transmission expansion.


2
    https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/05/24/15.1.4.3-ERCOT-Comments-on-NPRR1325-and-PGRR145.pdf
3
    (Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication, p 38

                                               Page 2 of 8
 Coincident Peak Methodology
       GRIT’s members previously supported retaining CP as the foundation for transmission cost
allocation while expanding the existing methodology in a targeted manner to account for winter
risk. If the Commission proceeds with a 12CP framework, using a blended approach of contracted
demand with actual demand encourages flexibility. Cost allocation should reflect the relationship
between customer demand and the transmission facilities required to serve that demand. Aurora
Energy Research’s resource adequacy analysis similarly indicates that system stress is not evenly
distributed across the calendar.4 Under average weather assumptions, Aurora found conditions
tightening principally during summer and winter, while spring and fall shoulder month conditions
generally remained stable because of lower demand and higher renewable production. Resource
adequacy and transmission planning are distinct, but the analysis reinforces the need to evaluate
whether equal monthly weighting reflects ERCOT’s actual operating and planning conditions.
       GRIT recommends using a blended approach that combines contracted demand with actual
12CP performance to determine minimum billing. Seasonal weighting may warrant further
consideration, but additional analysis is needed before adoption. For instance, the Commission
should evaluate whether changing the relative weight of seasonal peaks would shift customer
behavior in ways that create new system peaks or new transmission investment.


Residential Access
       GRIT supports the comments filed by Base Power Company in Project No. 58000. The
proposed rule reforms how transmission costs are allocated upstream, but it leaves the
downstream billing structure untouched. GRIT joins Base in asking the Commission to adopt the
opt-in, portfolio-level demand-based billing election proposed in Project No. 58484 —
implemented through the annual allocation factor update under amended §25.193 with electing
REPs required to intermediate the demand charge rather than pass it directly to residential
customers. Short of that, GRIT asks the Commission to designate this residential billing
asymmetry an open item for priority resolution and direct Staff to develop an implementation
proposal on a defined schedule.


4
 https://www.ercot.com/files/MarketNotice/2025/11/310252/Aurora%20Assessment%20of%20Resource%20Adequ
acy%20Needs%20in%20ERCOT%20Region%20and%20Impact%20of%20Market%20Design%20Changes%20%2
82025.11.10%29.pdf

 RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT
   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
       different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different
       NCP demands?
       GRIT agrees that the values associated with large load minimum billing demand should be
different for customers with different characteristics. Any distinction should reflect the nature of
the transmission service required rather than customer size alone. A customer that requires firm
service for its full contracted demand should generally bear a higher minimum billing obligation
than a customer that accepts a lower withdrawal limit and provides dependable onsite capacity or
curtailment capability. Applying the same requirement to both would fail to reflect their materially
different contributions to transmission costs, assuming planning processes are updated to reflect
contributions from onsite capacity or curtailment capability.
   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be fixed for 20 years as proposed,
       reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or extended to a longer time period?
       GRIT recommends that the minimum billing demand decline in phases rather than remain
fixed at 100 percent of contracted peak demand for 20 years. This recommendation should be
considered together with both Senate Bill 6 and the Commission’s proposed large load
interconnection standards in Project No. 58481, which already establish substantial protections
against stranded infrastructure costs. Senate Bill 6 requires uniform financial commitments and
contemplates the release of security as a customer meets load ramp milestones, sustains operations,
withdraws requested capacity, or permits that capacity to be reallocated. The Commission’s
proposal would implement those protections through per-megawatt financial security, a non-
refundable interconnection fee, full payment of direct interconnection costs through CIAC, and
financial security for significant equipment, services, and system upgrades. The proposal would
also apply financial security to outstanding costs when capacity is withdrawn or remains unused
and would release a portion of the remaining security as the customer meets phased energization
milestones and establishes sustained operations.
       Taken    together,   these   measures       already   address   development,   cancellation,
underutilization, and stranded-cost risks at multiple stages of the interconnection process. A
separate minimum billing demand may provide additional protection during the initial years of
service, but maintaining a 100-percent contracted-demand floor for 20 years risks duplicating

                                            Page 4 of 8
 protections after the underlying exposure has materially declined. A phased minimum would more
closely align the billing obligation with the remaining risk while continuing to protect existing
ratepayers.


    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
        lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand?
        GRIT submits that any approach should provide a reasonable balance between protecting
against underutilized infrastructure and preserving incentives for demand flexibility and peak
reduction with on-site generation. Rather than establishing contracted peak demand as an absolute
floor, the minimum billing demand could blend that measure with the customer’s actual 12CP
demand, with the weight assigned to contracted peak demand declining over time. Including actual
12CP performance in the calculation would preserve a meaningful incentive for customers to
reduce grid withdrawal during coincident peaks, while still providing a reliable contribution
toward transmission costs.
        A minimum significantly below 100% would also be consistent with several recently
approved large load tariff structures. AEP Ohio’s approved data-center tariff utilizes an 85%
minimum billing demand construct tied to contract capacity5, Dominion Energy Virginia’s GS-5
rate class applies an 85 percent minimum to contracted transmission and distribution demand6, and
Indiana Michigan Power’s large load tariff sets the minimum monthly billing demand as the
greater of 80% of the capacity contracted by the customer, or 80% of the customer’s highest
monthly demand over the prior eleven months7. More broadly, national surveys of emerging
hyperscale and data center tariff structures have observed that minimum billing demand
obligations in the range of approximately 75% to 90% have increasingly become the prevailing
framework for large load tariff design.8 These examples demonstrate that a minimum below 100%
can provide substantial protection against stranded infrastructure costs without eliminating the
value of reducing demand during the periods used to allocate transmission costs.




5
  AEP Ohio’s Data Center Tariff
6
  VA SCC Press Release on New GS-5 Rate Class
7
  Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission Order Approving I&M’s Industrial Power Tariff
8
  RMI Report on the Design of Large Load Tariffs

                                                Page 5 of 8
        GRIT encourages the Commission to carefully evaluate the potential reliability
implications associated with aggressive minimum demand constructs. ERCOT currently relies on
substantial flexible load and demand response participation during periods of system stress.
Excessively rigid minimum demand obligations may unintentionally reduce incentives for
participation in demand response programs, operational flexibility initiatives, and customer
investment in resiliency infrastructure and colocated generation resources capable of supporting
ERCOT’s reliability objectives.


   4. Should separate rate treatment apply to a large computational load?
       GRIT does not recommend separate rate treatment solely based on load type. Any
differentiation should be technology neutral and grounded in cost causation and demonstrated
system impacts, including contribution to system peaks and transmission upgrades directly
attributable to the customer. A customer’s flexibility, onsite resources, or ability to limit firm grid
withdrawal should also be reflected in the applicable rate treatment.


   5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve
       the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?
       GRIT recommends that batch-study transmission costs be assigned to a large load only to
the extent they are directly and reasonably attributable to that customer’s service request. The cost
allocation should reflect the customer’s firm service requirement, the incremental upgrades caused
by the interconnection, and any enforceable flexibility that could reduce or defer the need for those
upgrades.


   6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
       the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
       these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
       transmission planning studies?
GRIT recommends that reserved but unused capacity be reflected appropriately in resource
adequacy reports and transmission planning studies. Resource adequacy assessments should use
the customer’s expected energization schedule and projected load ramp, while transmission

                                             Page 6 of 8
 planning should reflect the level of firm service the customer is authorized to receive. ERCOT
should update those assumptions as projects meet or miss development milestones and as unused
capacity is reduced or reallocated. Any onsite generation, curtailment capability, or withdrawal
limit should be recognized where it is enforceable and sufficiently reliable for ERCOT to depend
upon in the applicable study.




CONCLUSION
       GRIT appreciates the opportunity to submit these responses to Commission Staff’s
recommendations on transmission cost recovery. As the Commission continues to move forward
with Project No. 58000 and related efforts, GRIT is committed to supporting the effort to ensure
improved grid reliability, resiliency, and stability.


                                               Respectfully submitted,

                                               By GRIT Member Companies:

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF GRIT COMMENTS
  •   A customer that installs dispatchable onsite generation, commits to a defined maximum
      grid withdrawal level, or agrees to reduce load during peak system conditions can reduce
      the amount of transmission service the grid must reliably provide. If those commitments
      are incorporated into planning studies, they can improve utilization of existing
      infrastructure and reduce the need for or timing of future transmission expansion.
  •   ERCOT’s PCLR and WLPUN constructs provide a workable foundation for a flexible
      transmission service option under which the customer’s withdrawal limit or ability to
      curtail is used in applicable planning models.
  •   For a qualified flexible customer, the minimum billing demand should be based on net
      firm withdrawal, i.e., the amount of demand that ERCOT and the applicable TSP must
      plan to serve after accounting for enforceable limits, curtailment, and approved onsite
      generation.
  •   A minimum billing demand below 100% can provide substantial protection against
      stranded infrastructure costs without eliminating the value of reducing demand during the
      periods used to allocate transmission costs.
  •   Rather than establishing contracted peak demand as an absolute floor, the minimum
      billing demand could blend that measure with the customer’s actual 12CP demand, with
      the weight assigned to contracted peak demand declining over time. This would more
      closely align the billing obligation with the remaining risk while continuing to protect
      existing ratepayers.
  •   GRIT joins Base Power Company in asking the Commission to adopt the opt-in,
      portfolio-level demand-based billing election proposed in Project No. 58484 —
      implemented through the annual allocation factor update under amended §25.193 with
      electing REPs required to intermediate the demand charge rather than pass it directly to
      residential customers.
